pedagogy.summary: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount: holding the whole constant, splitting each part into more (smaller) pieces multiplies both numerator and denominator without changing the quantity, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. The load-bearing insight, best seen on a fraction wall or bar, is that MORE pieces each SMALLER can total the same amount — which directly confronts the whole-number bias that '4/6 must be more than 2/3 because 4 > 2'. Teach the multiplicative structure with diagrams before any 'times top and bottom' rule.
bestPractices: Build equivalence by SPLITTING each part of a fixed bar (2/3 → split each third in two → 4/6) so the shaded amount visibly never changes
Use a fraction wall / stacked bars so equal rows align and equivalents line up
Confront the additive error explicitly — show that '+1 to top and bottom' (2/3 → 3/4) shifts the shaded amount
Confirm on a number line that equivalent fractions land on the SAME point
Compare shaded AREAS of identical wholes, never different-sized wholes, when judging equivalence
keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / stacked equal-length bars (canonical equivalence reference)
A single bar re-partitioned by splitting each part (2/3 → 4/6)
Number line with dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) showing the same point
Area model (identical rectangles shaded to the same amount)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — 4/6 judged more than 2/3 'because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces'
Different numbers must mean different amounts (denies equivalence)
Makes 'equivalents' by ADDING the same number to top and bottom (2/3 → 3/4)
Compares shaded amounts across different-sized wholes
Thinks changing only the numerator or only the denominator keeps the value

learn.summary: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount. Holding the whole constant, splitting each part into more (smaller) pieces multiplies both numerator and denominator without changing the quantity, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. The load-bearing insight, best seen on a fraction wall or bar, is that MORE pieces each SMALLER can total the same amount, which confronts the whole-number bias that '4/6 must be more than 2/3 because 4 > 2'. Teach the multiplicative structure with diagrams before any 'times top and bottom' rule.

activities.title: Split each part of a fixed bar (2/3 becomes 4/6)
feedback: If the child says the second bar has more chocolate, lay the 2/3 bar directly over the 4/6 bar so the shaded lengths coincide; the pieces are smaller but the shaded strip is identical.

If the child changes only the numerator or only the denominator and expects the same amount, shade that fraction on an identical bar and compare: the shaded length differs, so both parts must be multiplied by the same number.
If the child offers 3/4 as equal to 2/3, shade 3/4 on an identical bar and align it with 2/3: the shaded length is clearly longer, so adding is not the same as splitting.
Prompt: 'Did the amount of chocolate change when you drew the splitting lines? What changed and what stayed the same?'
Reinforce: both the number of parts and the number shaded were multiplied by the same number, so the fraction's value did not change.
activities.rationale: Making and watching the split while the shaded length stays fixed lets equivalence be felt as 'same amount, more cuts', and directly contrasts changing one part, and the additive error, with the multiplicative structure. An interactive version (a 'split every part into ___' control that cleaves each part live while the symbol updates 4/6, 6/9, with an 'add 1 to top and bottom' button that visibly shifts the strip) may make the mechanism more concrete, but drawing the splits on paper serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Shade two of three equal parts of a bar to show 2/3.
Split every third into two equal pieces by drawing a line through each part; count that four of six parts are now shaded and write 4/6.
Describe what happened to the length of shaded strip: it did not grow or shrink, there are just more lines.
Keep splitting to generate the family: split each part into three for 6/9, into four for 8/12; each time check the shaded strip stays the same length.

Test changing only one number: on an identical bar change only the bottom number (2/3 to 2/6) or only the top number (2/3 to 3/3) and shade it; check that the shaded amount changes, so changing just one part does NOT make an equivalent fraction.
Try the trap: add one to the top and one to the bottom (2/3 to 3/4) and shade 3/4 of an identical bar; compare the shaded length with the original 2/3.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting each part (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) makes more, smaller pieces that cover exactly the same amount; for fractions like 2/3, changing only one of the two numbers, or adding one to each, shifts the amount, so neither is a way to make an equivalent fraction.

activities.title: Fraction wall: which rows line up
feedback: If the child reads only the numbers, redirect attention to where each bar ends relative to the shared vertical line.
Ask: 'These have different numbers but reach the same line. What does that tell you about the amount?'
If the child cannot see why rows align, connect back to splitting: a third split into two gives two sixths, which is why 2/3 and 4/6 reach the same line.
activities.rationale: The fraction wall is the canonical static reference for equivalence; tapping or tracing a row shows which fractions align. It shows the result rather than generating the split-each-part mechanism, so pair it with the splitting activity.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Use a fraction wall of stacked equal-length rows (halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, ninths) and find where rows end at the same vertical line.
Identify equivalents by alignment: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6, and 2/3 = 4/6.
Explain in words why two fractions that reach the same line are equal (they cover the same length of the identical whole).
Check a non-example: does 2/3 line up with 3/4? Note it does not, so they are not equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction wall is a reliable reference: fractions that cover the same length of the identical whole name the same amount, regardless of how many pieces.

activities.title: Same point on the number line
feedback: If the child expects two different points, count the sixths across to 4/6 and the thirds across to 2/3 and show the marks fall together.
Ask: 'If they are at the same point, how much of the distance from 0 to 1 does each cover?'
Connect to the bar: the same length on the bar becomes the same point on the line.
activities.rationale: Showing equivalents coinciding at one point addresses whole-number bias, where a child compares numerators and denominators separately, by making magnitude the object of attention. Dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) makes the shared point concrete.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.
learnerActions: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and mark thirds above it (1/3, 2/3).
On the same line, mark sixths below it (1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6, including 4/6 against 2/3).
Place 2/3 and 4/6 and check whether they land on the same point or different points.
Repeat with 1/2 and 2/4 (marking halves and quarters) to confirm they coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude and land on the same point of a number line, independent of how the line is partitioned.

activities.title: Sort, match and complete equivalents
feedback: If 3/4 is placed with the equivalents, ask the child to shade 3/4 and 2/3 on identical bars and compare the lengths.
For a missing-value error, return to splitting: 2/3 with each part split into two gives 4/6, so the numerator is 4.
Note: these matching and completion tasks check classification and completion; they do not by themselves build the multiplicative structure, so use them after the diagram work above.
activities.rationale: Recognition and completion tasks assess equivalence and can catch the additive error, but they test rather than construct the underlying structure. Keep them as consolidation, not as the primary teaching.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Match pairs of equivalent fractions (for example 1/2 with 2/4, 2/3 with 4/6), justifying each with a quick diagram.
Complete the missing value: 2/3 = __/6, and explain how the splitting gives the answer.
Sort a set into 'equivalent to 2/3' and 'not equivalent', deliberately including the additive trap 3/4, and explain why 3/4 does not belong.
When comparing shaded amounts, always use identical-sized wholes, never different-sized wholes.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying and completing equivalents consolidates the idea; the additive trap, together with a required explanation, checks whether the child multiplies both parts rather than adding.

activities.title: Predict, overlay, explain (diagnostic)
feedback: If the prediction is '4/6 is more because 4 > 2', after overlaying the bars, split each third in front of the child to show four smaller sixths covering the same length.
If the child says the two 'just look the same', push for the mechanism: each third was split in two, so the amount could not change.
If the child denies they can be equal because the numbers differ, show them landing on the same number-line point and name both as one amount.

A full response states 2/3 = 4/6, justifies by holding the whole constant and splitting each part, rejects the additive error, generates another equivalent, and confirms the same point on a number line. A partial response agrees the shaded amounts match but explains it only as 'they look the same' or by counting, without the split-each-part mechanism. A gap response says the fraction with bigger numbers is more or denies equivalence is possible.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a required reason surfaces whole-number bias, no-equivalence and additive misconceptions even when a rehearsed child guesses 'same'. Comparing only identical wholes keeps the portion comparison valid; the number-line step confirms shared magnitude.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.

Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.
learnerActions: Look at two identical bars held apart: one shaded 2/3, one shaded 4/6.
Predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME as 2/3, and state a reason BEFORE checking.
Slide the second bar onto the first and observe whether the shaded regions coincide.
Respond to a claim: 'Mia says 4/6 is more because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces.' Explain why she is wrong.
Generate one further fraction equal to 2/3 using a diagram and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: The stated reason, not just the final answer, reveals whether the child holds the whole constant and compares the shaded amount, or falls into whole-number or additive thinking.

constraints: When comparing represented portions (shaded areas or bar lengths), always use identical-sized wholes; comparing shaded amounts across different-sized wholes invalidates the equivalence judgement. As numbers on a number line, equivalent fractions remain comparable and coincide at one point.
Teach the multiplicative structure (splitting each part, multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) with diagrams BEFORE introducing any 'times top and bottom' rule.

Both numerator and denominator must be multiplied by the same number: for fractions less than one, such as 2/3, adding one to each (2/3 to 3/4) or changing only one of the two numbers shifts the shaded amount and does not make an equivalent fraction. (Adding one to each keeps the amount the same only when the fraction is a whole, e.g. 3/3 to 4/4, so it is not a valid rule.)
Matching, sorting and fill-in-the-blank tasks consolidate and check classification/completion but do not on their own build the underlying structure; use them after diagram-based construction.
A fraction wall shows which fractions align but does not itself demonstrate the split-each-part mechanism; pair it with active splitting.
Suitable for ages 7-8 (small denominators); the goal is recognising and showing equivalence with diagrams, not symbolic manipulation in isolation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original catalog rated a conversation/persona format as 'adds little' and a third dimension as 'decorative' for this planar area/length idea. These were catalog fit judgements and are not asserted here as universal claims: a discussion may still support reasoning and a 3D model is simply not needed for a planar length/area concept; the stated objective is diagram-based construction of equivalence.

Arithmetic check: 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9 = 8/12 (multiplying both parts by 2, 3, 4); 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. The additive trap 2/3 to 3/4 is correctly presented as NOT equivalent (3/4 = 0.75 > 2/3 approximately 0.667). No numerical errors found.

The source pedagogy also listed the misconception that changing only the numerator or only the denominator preserves value; this is now explicitly addressed in the splitting activity (e.g. 2/3 to 2/6), alongside the additive trap.

The IES source claim quotes the student misconception 'thinking 3/8 > 3/5' (in reality 3/8 < 3/5); it is retained verbatim only as a description of the misconception in sourceClaims and is never offered to a learner as a valid comparison.
The source row referenced internal prerequisite reteach ids for the whole-number and no-equivalence misconceptions; these are internal identifiers and have been omitted from learner-facing guidance.

assess.poeTask: Show the two fractions un-overlaid: a bar shaded 2/3 and an identical bar shaded 4/6, held apart. Ask the child to predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME amount as 2/3, and to say why before checking. A whole-number-biased child predicts '4/6 is more, because 4 > 2'. Then slide the second bar onto the first — the shaded regions coincide exactly. The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Draw a line splitting each of the three parts of the first bar in half. What fraction is shaded now, and did the amount of chocolate change?
Is 2/3 the same as 3/4? Someone got 3/4 by adding one to the top and one to the bottom — what would you say?
Find another fraction equal to 2/3 using a diagram. How do you know it's equal?
On a number line from 0 to 1, would 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point or different points? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: They are equal — 2/3 = 4/6. The same amount of chocolate is shaded on both bars; the second bar just has each third split into two, so four smaller sixths cover exactly the same length as two thirds. Mia is wrong: more pieces are each smaller, so the total amount is the same.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — the fraction with bigger numbers/more pieces is judged to be more (4/6 > 2/3 because 4 > 2 and 6 > 3)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two identical bars so the shaded lengths coincide; split each third to generate the sixths in front of the child so the amount is seen not to change
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/6 is more, because 4 is more than 2 and it has more pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 4/6 is more chocolate and points to the larger numbers or the greater number of shaded pieces

errorPatterns.pattern: No-equivalence — different numbers must name different amounts, so 2/3 and 4/6 'can't be the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 2/3 and 4/6 landing on the same point on a number line and covering the same length on the wall; name both as one amount
errorPatterns.distractor: They must be different — the two fractions have different numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists they must differ because the fractions are written with different numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — makes 'equivalents' by adding the same number to top and bottom (2/3 = 3/4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast +1-to-each (shifts the shaded strip) with split-each-part (leaves it fixed); establish that both parts must be MULTIPLIED
errorPatterns.distractor: 2/3 = 3/4 — I added one to the top and one to the bottom.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Generates an equivalent by +1 to each, or agrees 2/3 = 3/4

responseLevels.gap: Says the fraction with bigger numbers is more (4/6 > 2/3), or denies that two differently-written fractions can be equal.
responseLevels.full: States 2/3 = 4/6 and justifies by holding the whole constant and splitting each part (multiplicative), rejects the additive error, generates a further equivalent, and confirms on a number line that they share the same point.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees 2/3 and 4/6 shade the same amount when shown the diagram, but explains it as 'they just look the same' or by counting, without the split-each-part mechanism; may still make equivalents by adding, or falter when the whole isn't drawn.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two identical chocolate bars. The first is split into three equal parts with two of them shaded (2/3). The second is split into six equal parts with four of them shaded (4/6). Mia says 4/6 is more chocolate, because 4 is more than 2 and there are more pieces. Is she right? How much of each bar is shaded, and WHY are they the same or different?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-biased child says 4/6 > 2/3 'because 4 > 2 / more pieces'. Correct reasoning holds the identical whole constant and compares shaded amount, recognising that splitting each part (multiplying numerator AND denominator) leaves the amount unchanged — the reason (tier 2) exposes the bias and the additive error even when a rehearsed child guesses 'same'.

sources.claim: Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.
